name: Gothic
summary: Pointed arches, ribbed vaults and flying buttresses turn the stone wall into a skeleton, and the freed walls become coloured glass. Chartres, Reims and Amiens set the height record that every later cathedral tried to beat.

philosophy.core_thesis: A building is a stone skeleton that lifts the eye to heaven: the thrust of each vault is caught by a buttress, so that walls can dissolve into light.
design_principles: Draw every opening as a pointed arch, with a rise of 1.0 to 1.5 times the span, so that the thrust goes down and not out.
Cover each bay with a rib vault, and carry the ribs down on clustered shafts so that the vault line reaches the floor.
Catch the thrust of the high vault with flying buttresses outside the aisle roof, at about 45° to the wall.
Raise the nave to a height of 2 to 3.5 times its width, from 30 to 48m under the vault, in three tiers: arcade, triforium, clerestory.
Give the upper wall to glass: windows fill 60 to 80% of the clerestory wall, divided by stone tracery.
Repeat the bay at 5 to 7m along the whole nave, so that the eye is led to the altar by the rhythm of the piers.
anti_patterns: Round arches and heavy plain walls with small openings
Flat ceilings or timber trusses left open over the nave
Classical orders, pediments or symmetrical Roman porticos
Wide, low proportions that stop the vertical lift
Smooth, bare stone with no moulding or tracery
Clear plain glass with no tracery or colour

massing.form: A long cross-shaped plan with a high nave, lower aisles and a polygonal apse; twin west towers of 60 to 120m and a crossing spire.
massing.proportion: Strongly vertical: the nave is 2 to 3.5 times higher than wide, and spires add a further 1 to 2 times the tower width.
massing.roof: A steep timber roof of 50 to 60° under lead or slate, with pinnacles, gables and a lead-covered spire.
massing.relation_to_ground: The building sits on a stepped plinth in the town square; three deep portals open the west front, with a rose window above.

structure.system: Load-bearing stone masonry with rib vaults, pointed arches and external flying buttresses.
structure.span_and_module: A nave bay of 5 to 7m wide and 6 to 8m long under a rib vault; the nave span is 12 to 16m.
structure.expression: Every thrust path is shown: ribs, shafts, buttresses and pinnacles are the structure and the decoration at once.

materials.finish: Carved by hand and weathered: sharp tracery in pale stone, and glass in deep reds and blues.

facade.composition: A west front in three vertical bays with three portals, a gallery of kings and a rose window, framed by two towers.
facade.openings: Pointed lancets, rose windows and traceried windows, with the glass share of the upper wall at 60 to 80%.
facade.solid_to_void: On the nave wall, 25–40% solid; on the west front, 55–70% solid.

light_and_space.daylight: Coloured light falls from the clerestory and the rose window, and fills the dim nave with moving patches of red and blue.
light_and_space.spatial_sequence: A dark narthex opens to a tall nave, then the crossing, the choir and the bright apse: the route runs east, to the light.
light_and_space.interior_character: Clustered columns, rib vaults, a triforium gallery, carved capitals and a stone floor; the eye goes up.

ornament.attitude: Ornament is structure made visible and made holy: tracery, crockets and carved figures grow out of the load path.

rules.rule: Make the nave height 2 to 3 times its width, and set the bay on a ratio of 1:2 in plan.
Repeat the bay, with its pier, arch and window, along the nave at a fixed module.
Put the portal, the nave and the high altar on one east–west axis, with a twin-tower west front.
Fill the clerestory and the rose window with stained glass, and keep the aisles dim.
Rank the central portal and rose above the side portals, and the nave above the aisles.
Make the interior tower over the person: vault heights of 30 to 48m.

images.title: Chartres Cathedral, central portal of the west façade
images.credit: Anne C. Richardson, Jim Womack (Vanderbilt ACT)

emotion.target_response: Awe and elevation: the viewer feels small under a stone sky that is full of coloured light.

avoid_when: The brief asks for a low, light, modern building or a flat roof.
The budget cannot pay for hand-carved stone and stained glass.

modifiers.how: Swap the pointed arch for a semicircle, the rib vault for a barrel or dome, and the tracery for orders on a ratio of 1:2 or 2:3.

sources.title: Paul Frankl, Gothic Architecture (Yale University Press, 2000; rev. Paul Crossley)
